title: NLP Evidence
text:
Supporting term exploration
The earlier TF-IDF workflow used one-word and two-word terms, minimum document frequency two, maximum document frequency 90%, and English plus domain stop words. Leading saved terms include ai, business, ll, models, and time. The contraction fragment ll and generic terms show why term weights require review. We do not treat TF-IDF rankings as skill-demand estimates.
Our final segmentation uses 37 recurring skills from combined evidence. A next improvement is a human-labeled extraction evaluation covering synonyms, negation, and required-versus-preferred language.

title: Final Recommendations
text:
We recommend a staged career plan. First, search for early-career analytics and data roles in software publishers and match each application to demonstrated SQL, Python, modeling, and visualization work. Examples of search titles include Data Analyst, Business Intelligence Analyst, Junior Analytics Engineer, and Junior Data Scientist. These are proposed search terms, not a claim that the ten-posting sample contains those entry-level vacancies.
Treat ML engineering, MLOps, applied-science, and AI architecture work as longer-term options. The six-posting AI and ML segment signals a different skill combination, while the reported experience requirements limit immediate accessibility. Broader searches can be a next step without changing the historical scope of this project.

title: Final Recommendations
text:
A practical screening process
For each vacancy, check explicit minimum experience, responsibilities, required versus preferred skills, location or remote arrangements, and disclosed compensation. Record missing information as unknown. Evaluate skills through specific artifacts and examples rather than a single readiness percentage. Compare pay only when experience level, location, and disclosure coverage are sufficiently similar.
California and New York, and the employers represented in the sample, provide starting points for exploration. Counts alone do not justify relocation, rank workplace quality, or establish current hiring activity. Verify fresh postings before investing time in an application.

title: Final Recommendations
text:
Our 90 day development plan
Days 1–30: demonstrate the foundation. Refactor the market-analysis workflow into reusable Python components. Document the data model, validate joins and missing values, and present an analysis with SQL and clear visualizations. Produce a reproducible portfolio case study with an environment file and a concise account of decisions.
Days 31–60: strengthen Machine Learning and MLOps. Build a second workflow on a dataset large enough for appropriate evaluation. Track experiments, preserve model versions, and explain validation choices and limitations. Produce evaluation results, a model card, and reproducible training or analysis instructions. The current ten-posting corpus remains a descriptive case study.
Days 61–90: show deployment and applied NLP. Package one small project, demonstrate cloud storage and deployment, and improve the description skill extractor. Manually review a labeled set of job descriptions and measure extraction errors before adding synonyms. Produce a working demonstration, deployment notes, and an error analysis.

title: Final Recommendations
text:
Measures of progress
Our proposed targets are two documented portfolio case studies, one cloud demonstration, and at least three revised self-ratings supported by artifacts. Course completion alone will not increase a rating. Once the first portfolio project is ready, review each cycle of 20 targeted applications to assess whether title choices, evidence, and application materials need adjustment. These are planned actions, not completed achievements or predicted outcomes.

title: Career Evaluation Logic
text:
Our evaluation connects four kinds of evidence to one career decision.

We first check each vacancy’s experience and practical constraints. We then compare its responsibilities and requested skills with concrete portfolio evidence. Salary is supporting context, with its reporting coverage shown. We use the segmentation to organize the search, not to assign a hiring probability.
The product does not aggregate pay, accessibility, and fit into one weighted score. Its final analytical track is segmentation. Each retained binary skill contributes equally to Jaccard similarity, and the role-family recommendation is explained through visible skill counts and accessibility limits.
The final analytics documents the variables, selection rule, evaluation results, restoration checks, and career interpretation. The recommendations turn that evidence into a 90-day development plan.

title: Market Baseline
text: The retained sample describes a narrow set of advertised roles, with substantially more adjacent technical roles than exact Data Scientist titles.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Demand and geography
Monthly counts are one in May, one in June, four in July, two in August, and two in September. These small counts do not establish market growth or seasonality. The role mix consists of four AI technical postings, two data-science-adjacent postings, and one each in core data science, machine learning, applied or decision science, and analytics engineering.
California accounts for five postings and New York for two. Colorado, Indiana, and Massachusetts contribute one each. C3 Iot, Klaviyo, and Workday have two postings apiece; Guidewire Software, Microsoft, Sigma Computing, and Theoris Group have one each. These are search leads, not employer-quality or cost-of-living-adjusted location rankings.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Pay and accessibility
All seven salary observations belong to adjacent roles. The sole core Data Scientist posting has no usable pay, so the sample cannot estimate its typical salary. Both restored skill segments have a median minimum experience requirement of five years. That result and the senior-oriented titles indicate an accessibility barrier for a recent graduate; a stronger skill match does not remove it.
The two remote postings establish only an explicitly remote share of 20% in this sample. The other eight are not confirmed onsite. We therefore avoid a remote-versus-onsite market-share claim or a remote-status classifier.

title: Project Scope and Product Framing
text:
Our product helps college students and recent graduates plan a path into data science within U.S. Software Publishers, NAICS 2022 code 513210. We focus on skill readiness and distinguish explicit Data Scientist roles from adjacent analytics, AI, machine-learning, and architecture roles. Software publishing is the industry boundary; the adjacent titles are part of the same defined career pathway, not an expansion into other industries (U.S. Census Bureau, 2022).
Our decision: prioritize early-career versions of analytics and data roles while developing the production and cloud skills needed for longer-term AI and ML work. This is a learning and search strategy. The ten historical postings do not establish that entry-level vacancies are plentiful or that our current profile satisfies a specific employer’s requirements.

title: Project Scope and Product Framing
text:
The question our product answers
Within the audited 2024 software-publishing sample, which role segments best align with our current skills, what barriers affect accessibility, and which learning priorities should guide our next career decision?
The product combines a market baseline, a documented student profile, and an explainable segmentation analysis. A reader can inspect the evidence, identify relevant role families, compare their own demonstrated skills with the reported patterns, and choose a portfolio project. Salary, location, and experience provide context rather than a promise of an offer.

title: Project Scope and Product Framing
text:
Why this scope matters
Job titles hide meaningful differences in skill combinations. De Mauro et al. organize big-data work into job families and skill sets, supporting our decision to compare related roles without treating them as interchangeable (De Mauro et al., 2018).

title: Career Evaluation in Software Publishing
text:
Our Group 10 product uses ten audited U.S. job postings from May–September 2024 in Software Publishers, NAICS 513210, to connect market evidence with a student’s career decisions.
Our recommendation: use analytics and data roles as the nearer-term search direction, while building the Machine Learning, MLOps, and cloud evidence needed for longer-term AI and ML roles. The sample is senior-oriented, so this is a skill-development strategy rather than a claim of entry-level availability.

title: Data Preparation
text: Our final analysis uses ten distinct Lightcast job postings from May through September 2024 in U.S. Software Publishers. Earlier exploratory material used a different 2026 source. We exclude those observations from the final market findings, skill comparison, segmentation, and recommendations (AD688 Group 10, 2026; Lightcast, 2024).

title: Data Preparation
text:
Sample construction and restoration
The earlier Step 3 scope audit documented 72,498 source rows and 1,037 exact-industry records before the pathway and date restrictions. The approved cohort contains explicit Data Scientist, data-science-adjacent, applied or decision scientist, AI technical, machine-learning technical, and analytics engineer titles. Occupation codes provide supporting metadata; a generic software title does not qualify solely because its description mentions AI.
Our full-source restoration run scanned 72,498 rows and found all ten approved posting IDs. Using the original preparation code reproduced the archived baseline tables, skill-demand counts, model scores, and cluster membership. We then removed one false R-programming match caused by the phrase “R D team.” This reduced the recurring model features from 38 to 37 while preserving the ten-posting cohort and its six/four grouping.
The restoration holds the approved IDs and core or adjacent labels fixed using the saved description corpus. It verifies their source records and downstream results; it does not independently rerun the original inclusion and exclusion decisions for every other industry title. The 1,037-record industry count remains an earlier scope-audit figure.

title: Data Preparation
text:
Cleaning and missing values
The restored panel has one row per posting ID. We standardize dates, salaries, experience, locations, and skill labels. The skill bridge combines normalized source labels with controlled description-keyword matches and records their origin. Alias normalization prevents equivalent terms from counting twice in the model. A separate NLP workflow decodes HTML entities, removes markup and URLs, normalizes whitespace and case, and preserves technical symbols in ten nonempty descriptions.
Salary analysis uses seven usable annual salary-range midpoints. We preserve the other three as missing and do not infer pay from title or employer. An annual midpoint summarizes an advertised range rather than realized earnings or total compensation. Unknown remote and education values remain unknown. Posting IDs connect the panel, skill bridge, descriptions, and model results.

title: Skill Gap Analysis
text:
One completed self-assessment was available at the analysis cutoff. We use that documented student profile for our comparison and do not infer another member’s ratings. The scale is 1 beginner, 2 basic, 3 intermediate, 4 advanced, and 5 expert. Ratings are self-reported.
For each skill, we count distinct postings in our combined skill evidence, which includes source labels and description-keyword matches. A posting share of at least 50% maps to priority 5; 40–49% to 4; 30–39% to 3; 20–29% to 2; and below 20% to 1. The priority gap equals market priority minus our rating.
This is a project-defined learning scale. Demand frequency is not an employer’s required proficiency level, so the subtraction is an ordinal planning heuristic. A zero gap does not establish qualification, and a four-point gap does not measure four units of missing ability.

title: Skill Gap Analysis
text:
Why skill evidence sources differ
MLOps appears in five postings in the prepared skill bridge. Three postings carry an explicit source skill label, and three match the narrower NLP dictionary. The broader preparation rules also recognize MLOps within joined wording in two C3 Iot descriptions, explaining the additional combined-evidence matches. Calling all five “structured records” would be inaccurate.
Using only the three narrow text matches would lower the MLOps priority from 5 to 3 and its gap from 4 to 2. Machine Learning would then become the largest gap. Our final scorecard uses combined evidence consistently; the other seven profile skills have the same counts under the combined and narrow-text rules. The R-language correction changes none of these eight profile counts.
Our practical conclusion is to strengthen Machine Learning and MLOps, develop Python and cloud skills, and maintain SQL, Data Modeling, and Data Visualization. Requirements in a target vacancy and evidence from completed projects should guide the ordering of similar learning priorities.

title: Final Analytics
text: We use Option C, segmentation, to distinguish role families by their skill combinations and connect those differences to our student profile. The decision is which role family should guide our search and learning plan, considering skill fit, experience barriers, and reported pay. The model does not estimate hiring probability or a salary premium for individual skills.

title: Final Analytics
text:
Variables and method
Our input is the restored ten-posting panel and its prepared skill bridge. The bridge combines normalized source skill labels with controlled description-keyword matches. After removing one false R-language match, 37 skills occurring in at least three postings enter the binary feature matrix. These include technical, business, and communication skills. Each row is a posting; each feature records whether the skill appears at least once.
We use average-linkage hierarchical clustering with Jaccard distance, which compares shared skill presences without rewarding two postings for both omitting a skill. Each retained skill has equal weight. Salary, location, experience, employer identity, and our self-ratings are excluded from clustering and used for interpretation. We do not combine pay, accessibility, and fit into a weighted opportunity score.

The two-cluster solution is selected, with a silhouette of 0.291. Three clusters have the highest score, 0.327, but create a singleton. Four clusters create two singletons. Only two clusters pass the minimum-size rule.
Silhouette measures internal separation on a scale from negative one to one, with larger values indicating clearer separation and values near zero indicating overlap (scikit-learn developers, n.d.). Our result supports an exploratory comparison with overlapping skill profiles. It is not a prediction-accuracy measure or a test on unseen postings.

SQL, Python, and Data Visualization each appear in three of four Analytics and Data postings. These skills align with our intermediate ratings. Machine Learning appears in all six AI/ML Architecture postings, MLOps in five, and Generative AI in four. That combination overlaps with our larger development needs.
We therefore recommend Analytics and Data as our nearer-term role-family search direction, with AI/ML Architecture as a longer-term learning target. Both groups require a median minimum of five years of experience. This is a relative skill-fit judgment; we still need to find early-career vacancies and check their requirements individually.
The median pay difference cannot establish a reliable segment premium. Salary coverage is six of six in AI/ML Architecture and only one of four in Analytics and Data. We cannot infer that cluster membership or a particular skill causes higher compensation.

title: Final Analytics
text:
Verification and practical limits
The unmodified preparation code reproduces the archived scores of 0.283, 0.319, and 0.305. Removing the single false R match produces the final scores of 0.291, 0.327, and 0.311. Cluster membership and all eight profile skill counts remain unchanged. Our final build also checks exact agreement with the restored feature matrix and posting assignments.
This verifies computational continuity and the effect of one extraction correction. It does not establish stability under new postings, employer changes, or other feature rules. With only ten observations, the groups remain hypotheses for organizing a career search. A new vacancy requires direct review of its responsibilities, experience, location, and pay.

title: ML Methods
text:
We use unsupervised learning to examine whether the audited job postings form meaningful groups based on their required skills. Our goal is descriptive: we want to identify different career pathways within the selected software publisher market, not predict outcomes for the broader labor market.
Our final analytical track is Option C: segmentation. The model uses our prepared skill bridge, which combines normalized source skill labels with controlled description-keyword matches. It does not use source labels alone. After correcting a false R-language match in the phrase “R D team”, the model retains 37 skills that occur in at least three postings. Salary, experience, location, and our self-ratings are used for interpretation, not as clustering features. Every retained binary skill has equal weight in the Jaccard comparison.
Because our final panel contains only 10 postings, a supervised salary or hiring model would not support a credible train-test evaluation. We therefore use hierarchical clustering and treat the results as exploratory evidence.

title: ML Methods
text:
Model Data
#| label: ml-model-data
#| echo: true

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering
from sklearn.manifold import MDS
from sklearn.metrics import pairwise_distances
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

panel_path = Path("data/processed/step3/career_market_panel.csv")
skills_path = Path("data/processed/step3/career_market_skills.csv")
figure_dir = Path("figures/step3")
output_dir = Path("outputs/step3")

figure_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

market_panel = pd.read_csv(panel_path)
market_skills = pd.read_csv(skills_path)

if market_panel["JOB_ID"].duplicated().any():
    raise ValueError("The market panel must contain one row per JOB_ID.")

skill_aliases = {
    "Generative Artificial Intelligence": "Generative AI",
    "MLOps (Machine Learning Operations)": "MLOps",
    "Kafka": "Apache Kafka",
    "Docker (Software)": "Docker"
}

market_skills["MODEL_SKILL"] = market_skills["SKILL"].replace(
    skill_aliases
)

market_skills = market_skills.drop_duplicates(
    subset=["JOB_ID", "MODEL_SKILL"]
)

skill_frequency = (
    market_skills
    .groupby("MODEL_SKILL")["JOB_ID"]
    .nunique()
    .sort_values(ascending=False)
)

# Retain skills appearing in at least 3 of the 10 postings. This reduces the
# influence of one-off terms while keeping skills observed in at least 30% of
# the audited market panel.
model_skill_names = skill_frequency[
    skill_frequency >= 3
].index.tolist()

feature_matrix = (
    market_skills[
        market_skills["MODEL_SKILL"].isin(model_skill_names)
    ]
    .assign(PRESENT=1)
    .pivot_table(
        index="JOB_ID",
        columns="MODEL_SKILL",
        values="PRESENT",
        aggfunc="max",
        fill_value=0
    )
    .reindex(market_panel["JOB_ID"], fill_value=0)
)

if feature_matrix.shape[1] < 2:
    raise ValueError("Too few recurring skills are available for clustering.")

model_input_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Measure": [
        "Distinct postings",
        "Unique normalized skills",
        "Skills retained for modeling",
        "Minimum posting frequency"
    ],
    "Value": [
        market_panel["JOB_ID"].nunique(),
        market_skills["MODEL_SKILL"].nunique(),
        feature_matrix.shape[1],
        "3 postings (30%)"
    ]
})

Each row of the modeling matrix represents one job posting. Each retained skill is a binary feature: 1 means the posting lists the skill and 0 means it does not. We use Jaccard distance because it compares shared presences in binary data without treating two shared absences as evidence that postings are similar.

title: ML Methods
text:
Selecting the Number of Clusters
#| label: ml-cluster-selection
#| echo: true

distance_matrix = pairwise_distances(
    feature_matrix.to_numpy(dtype=bool),
    metric="jaccard"
)


def fit_agglomerative(distance_values, number_of_clusters):
    """Fit average-linkage clustering across scikit-learn versions."""
    try:
        model = AgglomerativeClustering(
            n_clusters=number_of_clusters,
            metric="precomputed",
            linkage="average"
        )
    except TypeError:
        model = AgglomerativeClustering(
            n_clusters=number_of_clusters,
            affinity="precomputed",
            linkage="average"
        )

    return model.fit_predict(distance_values)


candidate_results = []
candidate_labels = {}

for candidate_k in [2, 3, 4]:
    labels = fit_agglomerative(distance_matrix, candidate_k)
    label_counts = pd.Series(labels).value_counts()

    candidate_labels[candidate_k] = labels
    candidate_results.append({
        "Candidate Clusters": candidate_k,
        "Silhouette Score": silhouette_score(
            distance_matrix,
            labels,
            metric="precomputed"
        ),
        "Smallest Cluster": int(label_counts.min()),
        "Singleton Clusters": int((label_counts == 1).sum())
    })

model_comparison = pd.DataFrame(candidate_results)
model_comparison["Silhouette Score"] = model_comparison[
    "Silhouette Score"
].round(3)

model_comparison.to_csv(
    output_dir / "ml_model_comparison.csv",
    index=False
)

The corrected scores are 0.291 for two clusters, 0.327 for three, and 0.311 for four. The three-cluster solution has the highest silhouette score, but it creates a cluster containing only one posting. The four-cluster solution creates two single-posting clusters. We select the highest-scoring candidate with at least two postings in every group. Only the two-cluster solution passes this rule. It provides a less fragmented career comparison.
Silhouette measures internal separation, not prediction accuracy. A value of 0.291 indicates overlapping skill profiles rather than sharply separated market segments. The unmodified preparation script reproduces the archived scores of 0.283, 0.319, and 0.305. The correction removes one false R match; the final six/four membership remains unchanged. No claim of out-of-sample stability follows from reproducing saved outputs.

Final Cluster Solution
#| label: ml-final-clusters

selected_k = 2
raw_cluster_labels = candidate_labels[selected_k]

architecture_markers = [
    "Artificial Intelligence",
    "Machine Learning",
    "MLOps",
    "Solution Architecture",
    "Cloud Computing Architecture"
]

available_architecture_markers = [
    skill
    for skill in architecture_markers
    if skill in feature_matrix.columns
]

architecture_scores = {}

for cluster_number in sorted(set(raw_cluster_labels)):
    cluster_mask = raw_cluster_labels == cluster_number
    architecture_scores[cluster_number] = (
        feature_matrix.loc[
            cluster_mask,
            available_architecture_markers
        ]
        .mean()
        .mean()
    )

architecture_cluster_number = max(
    architecture_scores,
    key=architecture_scores.get
)

cluster_names = []

for cluster_number in raw_cluster_labels:
    if cluster_number == architecture_cluster_number:
        cluster_names.append("AI/ML Architecture")
    else:
        cluster_names.append("Analytics and Data")

clustered_panel = market_panel.copy()
clustered_panel["CLUSTER_NAME"] = cluster_names
clustered_panel["PLOT_ID"] = [
    f"J{number:02d}"
    for number in range(1, len(clustered_panel) + 1)
]

clustered_panel["IS_CORE"] = (
    clustered_panel["SCOPE_TIER"] == "Core"
).astype(int)

cluster_summary = (
    clustered_panel
    .groupby("CLUSTER_NAME")
    .agg(
        Postings=("JOB_ID", "nunique"),
        Core_Postings=("IS_CORE", "sum"),
        Salary_Observations=("SALARY_MIDPOINT_ANNUAL", "count"),
        Median_Reported_Salary=("SALARY_MIDPOINT_ANNUAL", "median"),
        Median_Minimum_Experience=("MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE", "median")
    )
    .reset_index()
    .rename(columns={
        "CLUSTER_NAME": "Cluster",
        "Core_Postings": "Core Postings",
        "Salary_Observations": "Salary Observations",
        "Median_Reported_Salary": "Median Reported Salary",
        "Median_Minimum_Experience": "Median Minimum Experience"
    })
)

cluster_summary["Median Reported Salary"] = cluster_summary[
    "Median Reported Salary"
].round(0)

cluster_summary["Median Minimum Experience"] = cluster_summary[
    "Median Minimum Experience"
].round(1)

cluster_assignments = clustered_panel[[
    "PLOT_ID",
    "TITLE_RAW",
    "ROLE_SEGMENT",
    "SCOPE_TIER",
    "CLUSTER_NAME"
]].rename(columns={
    "PLOT_ID": "Plot ID",
    "TITLE_RAW": "Job Title",
    "ROLE_SEGMENT": "Role Segment",
    "SCOPE_TIER": "Scope Tier",
    "CLUSTER_NAME": "Cluster"
})

cluster_summary.to_csv(
    output_dir / "ml_cluster_summary.csv",
    index=False

Visualizing the Cluster Structure
#| label: ml-cluster-map

import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly_theme import BLUE, NAVY, TEAL, apply_job_market_theme

try:
    mds_model = MDS(
        n_components=2,
        dissimilarity="precomputed",
        random_state=42,
        n_init=20,
        max_iter=1000,
        normalized_stress="auto"
    )
except TypeError:
    mds_model = MDS(
        n_components=2,
        dissimilarity="precomputed",
        random_state=42,
        n_init=20,
        max_iter=1000
    )

coordinates = mds_model.fit_transform(distance_matrix)

cluster_plot_data = clustered_panel[[
    "PLOT_ID",
    "TITLE_RAW",
    "ROLE_SEGMENT",
    "CLUSTER_NAME"
]].copy()

cluster_plot_data["MDS_1"] = coordinates[:, 0]
cluster_plot_data["MDS_2"] = coordinates[:, 1]

cluster_colors = {
    "AI/ML Architecture": TEAL,
    "Analytics and Data": BLUE
}

cluster_order = [
    "AI/ML Architecture",
    "Analytics and Data"
]

fig_clusters = go.Figure()

for cluster_name in cluster_order:
    cluster_rows = cluster_plot_data[
        cluster_plot_data["CLUSTER_NAME"] == cluster_name
    ]

    fig_clusters.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=cluster_rows["MDS_1"],
        y=cluster_rows["MDS_2"],
        mode="markers+text",
        name=cluster_name,
        text=cluster_rows["PLOT_ID"],
        textposition="top center",
        marker={
            "color": cluster_colors[cluster_name],
            "size": 18,
            "line": {"color": "white", "width": 1.5}
        },
        customdata=cluster_rows[[
            "TITLE_RAW",
            "ROLE_SEGMENT"
        ]].to_numpy(),
        hovertemplate=(
            "%{text}<br>"
            "%{customdata[0]}<br>"
            "Role segment: %{customdata[1]}"
            "<extra></extra>"
        )
    ))

apply_job_market_theme(
    fig_clusters,
    title="Skill-Based Job Clusters",
    subtitle=(
        "Two-group hierarchical clustering using recurring posting skills"
    ),
    x_title="MDS dimension 1",
    y_title="MDS dimension 2",
    note=(
        "Points that are closer together have more similar skill profiles; "
        "axis direction has no independent substantive meaning."
    ),
    height=650,
    showlegend=True,
    grid_axis="none"
)

fig_clusters.write_image(
    figure_dir / "ml_skill_clusters.png",

)



Two skill-based clusters of the audited job postings.


The map is a two-dimensional representation of the Jaccard distances used by the clustering model. The axes are positioning dimensions rather than measured job attributes, so only the relative distances and group membership should be interpreted.

Machine Learning appears in every AI/ML Architecture posting, while MLOps and Computer Science appear in five of the six. title: ML Methods
text:
Career Interpretation
The cluster results identify two different routes within our filtered market:

AI/ML Architecture emphasizes production-oriented machine learning, MLOps, cloud architecture, generative AI, and solution design. This pathway is attractive because these skills are common in the audited postings, but it currently has the largest overlap with the high-priority gaps identified in our skill-gap analysis.
Analytics and Data emphasizes SQL, visualization, predictive analysis, and business-facing applications. This pathway is closer to our current strengths in SQL, Data Modeling, and Data Visualization and is therefore our nearer-term role-family search direction. Both clusters have a median reported minimum experience of five years. We should investigate early-career versions of these roles; the observed vacancies do not establish entry-level accessibility.

The salary values do not support a reliable comparison between clusters. All six AI/ML Architecture postings report usable salary information, whereas only one of the four Analytics and Data postings does. We therefore report salary coverage and medians transparently but do not interpret the difference as a cluster-level compensation effect.

title: ML Methods
text:
Limitations
Our analysis uses only 10 postings, including one core Data Scientist posting, so the clusters may change if additional postings are added. Skill presence is also binary and does not measure the proficiency expected by an employer. The MDS chart simplifies many skill dimensions into two display dimensions, and its axes have no independent meaning. Consequently, the clusters are best used as an exploratory career-planning framework rather than a general market taxonomy or predictive model.

title: Career Strategy
text:
We recommend a staged career plan. First, search for early-career analytics and data roles in software publishers and match each application to demonstrated SQL, Python, modeling, and visualization work. Examples of search titles include Data Analyst, Business Intelligence Analyst, Junior Analytics Engineer, and Junior Data Scientist. These are proposed search terms, not a claim that the ten-posting sample contains those entry-level vacancies.
Treat ML engineering, MLOps, applied-science, and AI architecture work as longer-term options. The six-posting AI and ML segment signals a different skill combination, while the reported experience requirements limit immediate accessibility. Broader searches can be a next step without changing the historical scope of this project.

title: Career Strategy
text:
A practical screening process
For each vacancy, check explicit minimum experience, responsibilities, required versus preferred skills, location or remote arrangements, and disclosed compensation. Record missing information as unknown. Evaluate skills through specific artifacts and examples rather than a single readiness percentage. Compare pay only when experience level, location, and disclosure coverage are sufficiently similar.
California and New York, and the employers represented in the sample, provide starting points for exploration. Counts alone do not justify relocation, rank workplace quality, or establish current hiring activity. Verify fresh postings before investing time in an application.

title: Career Strategy
text:
Our 90 day development plan
Days 1–30: demonstrate the foundation. Refactor the market-analysis workflow into reusable Python components. Document the data model, validate joins and missing values, and present an analysis with SQL and clear visualizations. Produce a reproducible portfolio case study with an environment file and a concise account of decisions.
Days 31–60: strengthen Machine Learning and MLOps. Build a second workflow on a dataset large enough for appropriate evaluation. Track experiments, preserve model versions, and explain validation choices and limitations. Produce evaluation results, a model card, and reproducible training or analysis instructions. The current ten-posting corpus remains a descriptive case study.
Days 61–90: show deployment and applied NLP. Package one small project, demonstrate cloud storage and deployment, and improve the description skill extractor. Manually review a labeled set of job descriptions and measure extraction errors before adding synonyms. Produce a working demonstration, deployment notes, and an error analysis.

title: Career Strategy
text:
Measures of progress
Our proposed targets are two documented portfolio case studies, one cloud demonstration, and at least three revised self-ratings supported by artifacts. Course completion alone will not increase a rating. Once the first portfolio project is ready, review each cycle of 20 targeted applications to assess whether title choices, evidence, and application materials need adjustment. These are planned actions, not completed achievements or predicted outcomes.
